claims.text: A hybrid model combining nonlinear temperature-dependent corrections with defect-aware ab initio calibration will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr conductivity within ±10% of experiment.
The ±10% accuracy will apply in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The model will achieve the stated accuracy for specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Pristine and 1 wt.% oxygen-doped forms of bulk HfNbTaTiZr have defect levels quantified by preliminary structural analyses.
The proposed model will augment classical perfect-crystal conductivity equations with additive corrections and nonlinear interaction terms.
The correction terms will be calibrated using DFT calculations on SQS models containing oxygen impurities and common point defects.
Conductivity in the 0–200 K regime is dominated by defect- and impurity-level conduction.
Phonon scattering and defect activation prevail in the 300–1200 K regime.
Defect densities and oxygen distributions can be quantified by ab initio SQS simulations and experimental defect characterization.
Oxygen impurities and intrinsic point defects modify the local electronic structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
The local electronic-structure modifications caused by oxygen and point defects enhance electron scattering.
Combining nonlinear scattering corrections with defect-aware DFT calibration will correct deviations inherent in perfect-crystal analytical predictions.
Traditional analytical predictions typically assume perfect crystals and neglect defect and impurity scattering.
The model is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen content around 1 wt.% and to the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K intervals.
Predictions may not transfer to substantially different impurity contents or temperatures at which additional scattering phenomena dominate.
A deviation greater than ±10% at either 150 K or 350 K will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state includes both pristine and 1 wt.% oxygen-doped specimens, while the boundary limits applicability to oxygen levels around 1 wt.%, leaving the claimed applicability to the pristine specimen internally inconsistent or unclear.
